The INSEE chapter’s account of each:








Style
What it does
Consequence




B
binary, no standardisation
A county’s total weight is its neighbour count, so Taoyuan with 11 neighbours exerts 11 times Xinhuang’s pull


W
row standardisation
Every row sums to 1. Gives more weight to border counties, which have few neighbours


C
global standardisation, all weights scaled so they total \(n\)
Central counties with many neighbours take more external influence than border ones


U
uniform, all weights total 1
Same shape as C, different scale


S
variance stabilisation, Tiefelsdorf
Introduced to reduce the heterogeneity that differences in neighbour count create



The sum of all elements is exactly \(n = 88\) for W, C and S. The INSEE chapter gives this as the reason autocorrelation statistics computed from different matrices can be compared. U totals 1 by definition and B totals 448, the link count.
The row sums of S vary less than B, C and U and more than W: a coefficient of variation of 0.184 against 0.349 and 0.000. That is the reduction in heterogeneity S was designed for.
B, C and U share a coefficient of variation of exactly 0.349 because all three are the same binary matrix under a single scalar multiplier. They differ in scale and not in shape, so any statistic invariant to scale cannot tell them apart.
Moran’s I in Lesson 5 is computed from the weights list, so W and S will not give the same answer there.

4.4.1 Which style inverse distance weights should use
The obvious fix is to change style = "B" to style = "W", matching the chapter’s sentence. The INSEE chapter argues against doing that.
Inside Chapter 8 the question never arises, because rswm_ids is built, printed, and then never used: every lag in its section 8.9 runs on plain Queen contiguity or binary weights, so the distance decay computed in 8.7 is never applied to anything.
de Bellefon, Loonis and Le Gleut set out what row standardisation means and then add a caveat directly about this case:

Each weight \(w_{ij}\) can be interpreted as the fraction of spatial influence on observation \(i\) ascribable to \(j\). In contrast, such standardisation implies a certain degree of competition between neighbours: the fewer neighbours a zone has, the greater their weight. Moreover, when weights are inversely proportional to the distance between the zones, row standardisation makes them difficult to interpret.

Row standardisation divides by a row sum that is itself a function of distance, so the result mixes two things: how far a neighbour is, and how far all the other neighbours happen to be. Every county’s weights are forced to total 1 however far away its neighbours are, so the decay is preserved between one county’s neighbours and erased between counties.
The two produce lagged variables on different scales:

lag_B <- lag.listw(rswm_ids,   hunan$GDPPC)
lag_W <- lag.listw(rswm_ids_W, hunan$GDPPC)

tibble(quantity = c("GDPPC itself", "lag, style B", "lag, style W"),
       min = c(min(hunan$GDPPC), min(lag_B), min(lag_W)),
       max = c(max(hunan$GDPPC), max(lag_B), max(lag_W))) |>
  kable(digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))




quantity
min

[1] 0.7818471


The W version stays on the scale of GDPPC. The B version is a sum of yuan-per-kilometre terms, which cannot be read as a neighbourhood income or plotted against one, and the two still correlate closely enough that a map of either looks reasonable.
So the chapter’s code may be the better choice. Which style is right depends on the use: a neighbourhood mean comparable to GDPPC, as in §3.6.1, requires W, while preserving the distance decay at its true magnitude requires B. The text names one and the code does the other, so a reader cannot tell which was intended. That is the error, whichever style is correct.
This page uses W wherever a lagged value is compared against GDPPC.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
4.5 Graph-based neighbour definitions
Section 4.3 showed that a fixed band leaves counties with no neighbour below 60 km, which is why the chapter sets the band from the most isolated county in the province. The INSEE chapter covers a family of neighbour definitions where that cannot happen, built from the geometry of the point set rather than from a distance threshold: “they have the advantage that it leaves no unit without neighbours.”
All four are in spdep, and each applies a different rule. Delaunay triangulation connects points into triangles that maximise the minimum angle. The sphere of influence graph joins two counties when the circles centred on each, drawn out to its own nearest neighbour, overlap. Gabriel’s graph joins two counties when no third county falls inside the circle having them as its diameter. The relative neighbour graph joins two counties only when no third county is closer to both of them than they are to each other. Each is a subgraph of the one before it.

graphs <- list(
  "Delaunay"            = tri2nb(coords),
  "Sphere of influence" = graph2nb(soi.graph(tri2nb(coords), coords)),
  "Gabriel"             = graph2nb(gabrielneigh(coords), sym = TRUE),
  "Relative neighbour"  = graph2nb(relativeneigh(coords), sym = TRUE),
  "Queen contiguity"    = wm_q,
  "Fixed band, 62 km"   = wm_d62,
  "Adaptive, k = 6"     = knn6)

map_dfr(names(graphs), function(nm) {
  n <- graphs[[nm]]
  tibble(method = nm, links = sum(card(n)), `avg links` = mean(card(n)),
         min = min(card(n)), max = max(card(n)), isolated = sum(card(n) == 0))
}) |> kable(digits = 2)

None of the four graph methods isolates a county, as the INSEE chapter claims. Neither does Queen contiguity on this data, so the advantage is over the distance band rather than over contiguity, and only below 60 km does that distinction start to matter.
The graphs change the spread. Queen contiguity runs from 1 neighbour to 11; Delaunay runs from 3 to 9 and the sphere of influence from 2 to 9. Taoyuan’s 11 neighbours in §3.2.1 come from it being a large county surrounded by small ones, which the INSEE chapter names as a known property of contiguity: “a very large zone surrounded by smaller zones will have a far greater number of neighbours than its neighbouring zones.” The graph methods are built on the centroids and so do not inherit that.
The relative neighbour graph is much the sparsest at 2.70 links on average, which matches Toussaint’s design goal quoted in the INSEE chapter, that it “adapts better to data by requiring the fewest links.”

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(hunan$geometry, border = "lightgrey", main = "Delaunay")
plot(graphs$Delaunay, coords, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, add = TRUE, col = "red")
plot(hunan$geometry, border = "lightgrey", main = "Relative neighbour")
plot(graphs$`Relative neighbour`, coords, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, add = TRUE, col = "red")








The left panel shows the artefact these methods are known for. Delaunay spans the convex hull of the point set, so counties along the provincial border are joined to each other by long edges that run outside Hunan and across counties they do not touch. The INSEE chapter does not raise this, and it is the reason the sparser subgraphs exist: the relative neighbour graph on the right keeps 238 links against Delaunay’s 498, and the long border edges are the first to go.
These are Euclidean-only in R, which the INSEE chapter flags as their limitation: great circle distance is not available, so on a province the size of Hunan they inherit the same planar assumption §4.2 measured.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
4.6 Geographically weighted summary statistics
Section 3.6.3 computed a mean for each county’s neighbourhood instead of one mean for the whole province. Geographically weighted summary statistics work the same way, but the weighting and the neighbourhood are both adjustable. The window average uses uniform weights over the contiguity neighbours; gwss() lets the weights decay with distance and lets the neighbourhood be a fixed count or a fixed radius.
The last four content slides of the Lesson 4 deck cover these and their robust versions, and Chapter 8 stops before them. GWmodel::gwss() computes them, and the deck’s slide 21 table is exactly its output.
Bandwidth is set to 6 adaptive, which is the queen contiguity average of 5.09 neighbours plus the county itself, so these statistics cover about the same neighbourhood as Part 1.

hunan_sp <- as_Spatial(st_transform(hunan, 4547))
gw <- gwss(hunan_sp, vars = "GDPPC", bw = 6, kernel = "bisquare",
           adaptive = TRUE, longlat = FALSE, quantile = TRUE)
names(as.data.frame(gw$SDF))

[1] "GDPPC_LM"     "GDPPC_LSD"    "GDPPC_LVar"   "GDPPC_LSKe"   "GDPPC_LCV"   
[6] "GDPPC_Median" "GDPPC_IQR"    "GDPPC_QI"    


LM is the local mean, LSD the local standard deviation, LVar the variance, LSKe the skew and LCV the coefficient of variation; Median, IQR and QI are the robust three.
quantile = TRUE is required to get those last three. Without it gwss() returns only the first five and silently omits the median, IQR and quantile imbalance. There is no warning; the columns are simply absent, and code that goes on to read GDPPC_Median fails later with a message about the wrong thing.

gwr <- as.data.frame(gw$SDF)
hunan$gw_mean   <- gwr$GDPPC_LM
hunan$gw_median <- gwr$GDPPC_Median
hunan$gw_iqr    <- gwr$GDPPC_IQR

tibble(
  statistic = c("GW mean", "GW median"),
  min = c(min(hunan$gw_mean), min(hunan$gw_median)),
  max = c(max(hunan$gw_mean), max(hunan$gw_median))
) |> kable(digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5),

gap <- abs(hunan$gw_mean - hunan$gw_median)
cat("largest gap between GW mean and GW median:", round(max(gap)), "yuan at",
    hunan$County[which.max(gap)], "\n")

At Xinshao the local mean is 28447 and the local median 11286. One rich neighbour is carrying the mean and the median ignores it. Reading the mean alone would put Xinshao’s neighbourhood in the middle of the province’s distribution when most of it is near the bottom.

4.6.1 Kernel choice and the quantile imbalance
The quantile imbalance records where the local median sits between the local quartiles. Write that position as \(t = (\text{Med} - Q_1)/(Q_3 - Q_1)\), so \(t = 0\) puts the median on the lower quartile and \(t = 1\) on the upper. The deck’s formula then reduces to \(QI = 2t - 1\): negative means the median sits nearer the lower quartile, positive nearer the upper, and zero means it is centred. It divides by the weighted IQR, so it is undefined wherever that IQR is zero.
The bisquare kernel reaches exactly zero at the bandwidth, so at bw = 6 adaptive the outermost of the six points is given a weight of 0 and only five carry any weight. With that few, the weighted first and third quartiles can land on the same observation. A Gaussian kernel never assigns a zero weight, so every neighbour contributes something.

gw_g <- gwss(hunan_sp, vars = "GDPPC", bw = 6, kernel = "gaussian",
             adaptive = TRUE, longlat = FALSE, quantile = TRUE)
gwr_g <- as.data.frame(gw_g$SDF)
tibble(kernel = c("bisquare", "gaussian"),
       `IQR of 0` = c(sum(gwr$GDPPC_IQR == 0), sum(gwr_g$GDPPC_IQR == 0)),
       `NaN imbalance` = c(sum(is.nan(gwr$GDPPC_QI)), sum(is.nan(gwr_g$GDPPC_QI)))) |> kable()




kernel
IQR of 0
NaN imbalance




bisquare
10
10


gaussian
0
0





Ten counties against none. Under the Gaussian kernel the quantile imbalance runs from -0.777 to 0.632 across the province, so no county’s median sits at a quartile but several come close.
The bisquare kernel is the usual default and is the wrong default at a bandwidth this small. The failure surfaces as NaN in a column rather than as an error, the same shape as the style = "B" problem above.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
4.7 Lagged explanatory variables in regression
Chapter 8 computes four lagged variables and never says what they are used for. Grubesic and Rosso are a worked case. Their definition, the one the lecture puts on slide 15, excludes the county itself from its own lag:
\[[Wx]_i = \sum_{j \neq i} w_{ij} x_j\]
Section 3.6.1 follows that definition, and the two window versions in §3.6.3 and §3.6.4 are a deliberate departure from it.
Their use for it is as an explanatory variable rather than a mapped quantity. They contrast it with the more familiar model where the dependent variable is lagged:

rather than creating a multiplier effect as with spatially lagged dependent variables, spatial cross-regressive terms can be used directly in a standard regression framework. In other words, even ordinary least squares regressions would work with these data and not bias \(\gamma\).

So a lagged explanatory variable can go straight into an ordinary regression, where a lagged dependent variable cannot. They used a queen’s contiguity matrix to build theirs. Section 4.1 settled on the same default here for a different reason.
They also give a way to say how much lagging alters the picture: cut both the variable and its lag into tertiles and measure agreement. On Philadelphia census tracts they report 44% of tracts in the same tertile, with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.2.
The same measurement on Hunan:

tertile <- function(x) cut(x, breaks = quantile(x, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
                           include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
t_own <- tertile(hunan$GDPPC)
t_lag <- tertile(hunan$lag_GDPPC)
tab <- table(own = t_own, lagged = t_lag)
tab

      lagged
own    low mid high
  low   17   9    4
  mid    9  14    6
  high   4   6   19



po <- sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab)
pe <- sum(rowSums(tab) * colSums(tab)) / sum(tab)^2
tibble(study = c("Hunan GDPPC, this page", "Philadelphia amenity diversity, Grubesic and Rosso"),
       `same tertile` = c(po, 0.44),
       kappa = c((po - pe) / (1 - pe), 0.2)) |>
  kable(digits = 3)









study
same tertile
kappa




Hunan GDPPC, this page
0.568
0.352


Philadelphia amenity diversity, Grubesic and Rosso
0.440
0.200





A Hunan county aligns more closely with its surrounding neighbours than a Philadelphia tract does: 56.8% fall in the same tertile as their neighbourhood, against 44%. Cohen’s kappa, which discounts the agreement that would arise by chance alone, is 0.35 against 0.2. Neither is high. Even here, 43% of counties fall in a different tertile from the neighbourhood around them, and Lesson 5 identifies those as spatial outliers.
The paper connects its own figure to its result. In their models the lagged variable was not significant, every interaction term came back above p = 0.2, and the fit did not improve. They give their own concordance of 0.2 as part of the reason, and set one alternative beside it: “measures at the participant’s own census tract are sufficient to capture relevant neighbourhood characteristics.”

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
section: 4.8 The lag scatter and Moran’s I
text:
4.8 The lag scatter and Moran’s I
The spatial lag from section 3.6.1 is one step away from Lesson 5. Plotting each county’s GDPPC against its neighbourhood mean gives the scatter that Moran’s I summarises.

ggplot(hunan, aes(x = GDPPC, y = lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(hunan$GDPPC), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(hunan$lag_GDPPC), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "GDPPC (yuan)", y = "Spatially lagged GDPPC (yuan)",
       title = "County GDPPC against its neighbourhood mean",
       subtitle = "Queen contiguity, row standardised weights") +
  theme_minimal()









cor(hunan$GDPPC, hunan$lag_GDPPC)

[1] 0.4846051


The upward slope means prosperous counties tend to sit beside prosperous counties, with a Pearson correlation of 0.485.
The dashed lines mark the two means and split the counties into four groups: prosperous beside prosperous (top right), poor beside poor (bottom left), and the two mismatched groups off the diagonal. Lesson 5 names these four and tests which memberships are stronger than chance.
Every value on the vertical axis depends on the weights matrix built in Part 1.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
In Exercises 4 and 5, one variable, GDP per capita, was used to test whether counties with similar values are neighbours. This exercise uses six variables on information and communication technology (ICT), five of them in the clustering, for a different question: can the 55 townships of Shan State, Myanmar, be grouped into a small number of regions, each made of townships with similar access to ICT, and each a single connected piece of territory?
Such a grouping is called regionalisation or geographic segmentation. On slide 3, regions are defined as internally homogeneous and contiguous, which combines two requirements:

from cluster analysis, that the townships in a region are similar on the variables;
from spatial analysis, that a region is one connected piece, so that it can be mapped and managed as one area.

Part 1 is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 12: the data, exploratory analysis, conventional hierarchical clustering, the SKATER and ClustGeo methods of spatially constrained clustering, and the profiles of the clusters. Part 2 is a review of the chapter’s method, with the methods on the Lesson 6 slides that the chapter does not cover: REDCAP, the automatic zoning procedure (AZP) and max-p. Spatially constrained hierarchical clustering (SCHC) is included as well. It is not on the slides, and it is provided by the rgeoda package used for the other three.






NoteSources



The hands-on exercise is one chapter, assigned for Lesson 6:

Chapter 12: Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques

The Lesson 6 outline sets two papers as self-reading.








Reading
What it contributes
Used in




Assunção et al. (2006), “Efficient Regionalization Techniques for Socio-Economic Geographical Units Using Minimum Spanning Trees”
SKATER: the minimum spanning tree and the conditions for its uniqueness, the pruning of the tree into regions, attributes measured “in standard deviation units”, a one-district region in the unrestricted São Paulo result and the minimum-population restriction that removes it, a comparison with AZP, the sum of squared deviations within regions as the quality of a partition, and the debate on combining homogeneity with compactness
Part 2, 3.2, 4.2, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7


Chavent et al. (2018), “ClustGeo: an R package for hierarchical clustering with spatial constraints”
The Ward-like criterion on two dissimilarity matrices, the choice of α, the equivalence of hclustgeo() with hclust(method = "ward.D") on the transformed matrix, the two kinds of geographic matrix D1, and the proportion of explained pseudo-inertia
Part 2, 3.3, 4.3, 4.6



The outline also lists five references. All five are used on this page:








Reference
What it contributes

Rovan and Sambt (2003), “Socio-economic Differences Among Slovenian Municipalities: A Cluster Analysis Approach”
All variables standardised, with the remark that the method makes no distributional assumptions; the number of clusters read from jumps in the Ward merge heights; clusters named from their mean profiles
4.2, 4.4, 4.8

4.4

The rule of thumb k = √(n/2); cluster means expressed as a percentage of the overall mean; clusters described by variables that were not used to form them
4.4, 4.8


Jaya et al. (2019), “Clustering with spatial constraints: The case of diarrhea in Bandung city, Indonesia”
ClustGeo with a distance-based and a contiguity-based D1 on the same data, and the argument that the choice of D1 should follow how the phenomenon spreads

de Souza and Taconeli (2022), “Spatial and non-spatial clustering algorithms in the analysis of Brazilian educational data”
A Moran’s I test on each variable before clustering; one k for every method; ClustGeo with both kinds of D1 and SKATER compared on the same data; clusters cross-tabulated against official regions and compared by F tests; min-max scaling; the NbClust majority vote for the number of clusters
4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, 4.8



The outline’s “All About R” section has links to four web pages, and three of them are used on this page. The UC Business Analytics tutorial on hierarchical cluster analysis is the source of chapter sections 12.7.8 to 12.7.10, and is used in sections 3.1.8, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4. The spdep reference for skater() documents the population criterion used in section 4.5, and the ClustGeo introduction page documents the two kinds of D1 used in section 4.6.
The Lesson 6 slide deck, dated 18 September 2026, lists five methods. The chapter covers two of them, SKATER and ClustGeo. REDCAP (slides 9 to 12), AZP and max-p (slide 2) are covered in section 4.7.















The chapter
This page
Why
Where




Scale of the clustering variables
computes min-max and z-score versions in 12.7.3 and 12.7.4, then clusters on the raw rates
Part 1 follows the chapter; Part 2 repeats the analysis on z-scores
On the raw rates, mobile phone and TV account for 81% of the squared distance between townships and computer for 0.6%. Standardising changes the six clusters substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.32)
4.2


Ward’s method
picks Ward from agnes(), then runs hclust(method = "ward.D")
ward.D2, which is the method agnes() scored and the one hclustgeo() runs
agnes(method = "ward") and hclust(method = "ward.D2") build identical trees. ward.D applied to unsquared distances is a different algorithm, and it changes the cluster sizes
4.3


Spatial pattern of each variable
not tested
Moran’s I for each of the six rates, as de Souza and Taconeli (2022) do before clustering
Only radio and land line are significantly autocorrelated. TV and mobile phone, which have the most weight in the raw distances, show no significant spatial pattern
4.1


Number of clusters
k = 1 has the largest gap statistic, and 6 is taken as having “the largest gap statistic” after it
6 kept, with the evidence from five criteria listed
k = 1 has the largest gap. NbClust’s majority vote is 2. Ward’s merge heights, read as Rovan and Sambt (2003) read them, jump at 2, 4 and 6
4.4


SKATER singletons
six regions, two of them single townships, not discussed
the singletons identified, and a minimum number of households per region applied, as in Assunção et al. (2006)
Three of six SKATER regions on the standardised variables are single townships: Muse, Tachileik and Taunggyi
4.5


Geographic matrix D1 for ClustGeo
st_distance() between polygons
centroid distances and the neighbourhood matrix of Chavent et al. (2018) compared
The distance between two polygons that share a boundary is zero. All 132 neighbouring pairs, and only those pairs, have D1 = 0, so D1 gives every neighbour the same value, zero, whatever the distance between their centres
4.6


Contiguity of the result
reported from the map
counted
ClustGeo applies a soft constraint. The chapter’s α = 0.2 solution has six clusters in 18 separate pieces
4.6, 4.8


REDCAP, SCHC, AZP, max-p
not covered
computed with rgeoda and compared
Slides 2 and 10 to 12 list REDCAP, AZP and max-p; SCHC is added from rgeoda
4.7


Minimum spanning tree
mstree() without a seed
set.seed() before mstree()
mstree() starts from a random node. The tree is the same, but the printed order of its edges and the numbering of the SKATER groups change from run to run
3.2.3


Colours for six groups
rect.hclust(border = 2:5) and groups.colors with five colours
six colours
With fewer colours than groups, the colours are reused and two groups look like one
3.1.10, 3.2.4


Cluster profiles
the chapter profiles the non-spatial ClustGeo clusters (12.10)
the profiles are drawn for the spatially constrained clusters as well
The purpose of the chapter is the regions, and the non-spatial clusters are fragmented

2.1 Packages
rgeoda provides the four methods in section 4.7, and mclust provides the adjusted Rand index used in Part 2 to compare two sets of clusters.

pacman::p_load(spdep, tmap, sf, ClustGeo, rgeoda,
               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, GGally, mclust,
               knitr, tidyverse)







NoteHow the code works





The block uses one function:
pacman::p_load(...)                                       # pacman

p_load() installs any package that is missing and then attaches all of them, so one call replaces a series of install.packages() and library() calls.

Two of the packages define a function with the same name. spdep and rgeoda both have a skater(), and whichever package is attached later hides the other. This page therefore always writes spdep::skater() or rgeoda::skater() in full.

NoteHow the code works





The block uses three functions:
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
filter(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr

st_read() reads the shapefile into an sf data frame with one row per township. dsn is the folder and layer the file name without its extension. It prints a summary that begins with the full path of the data folder on the computer that renders the page, and the chunk option results: hide keeps that summary off the page.
filter() keeps the rows for which a condition is true. The condition here is ST %in% c("Shan (East)", "Shan (North)", "Shan (South)"), dissected below.
select(c(2:7)) keeps columns 2 to 7 by position, also dissected below.

What ST, DT and TS are
Myanmar is divided into states and regions, each state or region into districts, and each district into townships. The file has one row per township, 330 rows, and three of its columns record the state, the district and the township name of each row:

ST: state or region, for example Shan (North)

DT: district within the state, for example Mongmit

TS: township within the district, for example Mongmit. One township is one row of the file.



A district and a township can share a name, as Mongmit does. The file also splits Shan State into three parts, Shan (North), Shan (South) and Shan (East), and records each part in ST as if it were a separate state. That is why the filter has to name all three.

The same condition can be written without %in%, as one comparison per name joined by |, which means “or”:
filter(ST == "Shan (East)" | ST == "Shan (North)" | ST == "Shan (South)")
%in% compares whole values, so each name must match exactly, including the space and the brackets. ST %in% "Shan" matches 0 townships, because no value of ST is the word “Shan” on its own.
The select() line
select(c(2:7)) keeps columns by their position in the file, so the position of each column has to be known first. RStudio’s data viewer numbers the rows but not the columns, so the positions are easiest to read in the Console.
names() prints the column names in order. The number in square brackets at the start of each printed line is the position of the first name on that line:

A township with more households has more households with a radio, whatever the level of access. In section 12.4.3, each count is divided by the number of households and multiplied by 1,000, which gives the number of households per thousand that own the item.

  mutate(RADIO_PR = Radio / `Total households` * 1000,

The block uses two functions:
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
rename(.data, new_name = old_name, ...)                   # dplyr

mutate() adds new columns computed from existing ones. The chapter writes a separate mutate() call for each of the six rates. A single mutate() call with six arguments gives the same result.
A column name that contains a space has to be written between backticks, as in `Total households`. That is the reason for the rename() that follows.
rename() gives the columns short names without spaces, written new = old.
ict_derived[, 12:17] uses R’s square brackets, which pick part of a table in the form table[rows, columns]. Nothing before the comma means every row, and 12:17 after the comma means columns 12 to 17. mutate() adds the six rates after the eleven original columns, so they are columns 12 to 17:

The rates are per thousand households, so a value of 500 for TV_PR means that half of the households own a television. The chapter calls them penetration rates.









NoteWhy the counts are turned into rates



A township with more households has more households owning a radio, whatever the level of access. Dividing each count by the township’s number of households makes the townships comparable, and multiplying by 1,000 expresses the result per thousand households:
\[\text{penetration rate} = \frac{\text{households owning the item}}{\text{total households}} \times 1000\]


The rest of the exercise is built on these penetration rates. Their distributions, maps and correlations are examined in Part 1, five of them are used as the clustering variables, and every set of clusters and regions on this page is formed from those five.

As in section 12.5.2.1, the penetration rates are joined to the township polygons on the township code.

shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, ict_derived, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "TS_PCODE"))

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
3.1 Hierarchical cluster analysis
This section follows sections 12.5 to 12.7 of the chapter. The clustering in it uses five of the ICT rates, without the locations of the townships.

3.1.1 Distributions
The distributions show whether a variable is skewed or has outlying townships. Both affect how far apart townships appear in the clustering later. In section 12.5.1, the count of households with a radio is compared with the penetration rate, first with histograms and then with boxplots.

ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")














NoteHow the code works





The block uses two functions:
ggplot(data, aes(x))                                      # ggplot2
geom_histogram(bins, color, fill)                         # ggplot2

ggplot() names the data, and aes(x = RADIO) the column drawn along the horizontal axis. The + adds a layer to the chart.
geom_histogram(bins = 20) divides the range of RADIO into 20 equal bins and draws a bar for the number of townships in each. color sets the outline of the bars and fill their inside.





ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black",
               fill = "light blue")














NoteHow the code works






geom_boxplot() draws the median as the line inside the box, the middle half of the townships as the box, and as separate points any township more than 1.5 times the height of the box beyond it. Those points are the outliers.




The same two charts for the penetration rate:

ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")









ggplot(data = ict_derived,
       aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black",
               fill = "light blue")








The count is strongly right-skewed, and the boxplot marks three townships as outliers. The largest counts belong to the townships with the most households. The rate is much closer to symmetric, with one township, Ywangan, above 480 radios per thousand households. The chapter’s question is what the two charts reveal: the skew and the outliers in the count come mostly from township size, and dividing by the number of households removes most of both.
The chapter then draws the six penetration rates side by side, one histogram each:

radio <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

tv <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
             aes(x = `TV_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

llphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                  aes(x = `LLPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

mphone <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                 aes(x = `MPHONE_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

computer <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                   aes(x = `COMPUTER_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")

internet <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
                   aes(x = `INTERNET_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue")


ggarrange(radio, tv, llphone, mphone, computer, internet,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 2)














NoteHow the code works





The blocks use one new function:
ggarrange(..., ncol, nrow)                                # ggpubr

The first block stores each histogram under a name, radio, tv and so on, without drawing it.
ggarrange() draws the six stored charts together in a grid of three columns and two rows.




Radio, TV and mobile phone are roughly symmetric. Land line, computer and internet are right-skewed: most townships have few households with them, and a small number have many.
Three features of the charts are used later on this page:







Feature of the charts
Used in




The count of radios is right-skewed and the rate is close to symmetric, because larger townships have more households with every item
2.3, the reason for using rates


The ranges of the rates differ widely: 116 to 843 for TV, 3 to 92 for computer
3.1.5 and 4.2: on the raw rates, TV and mobile phone make up 81% of the squared distance between townships, and computer 0.6%


Ywangan has the highest radio rate, and computer, land line and internet have long right tails
3.2.4: Ywangan is one of the two single-township SKATER regions on the raw rates. 4.5: Tachileik, Muse and Taunggyi, the three highest computer rates, are the three single-township regions on z-scores





3.1.2 Choropleth maps
Maps show where in the state the high and low values of a rate are, which the histograms of section 3.1.1 cannot show. The first map in section 12.5.2.2 is a quick map of the radio penetration rate.

qtm(shan_sf, "RADIO_PR")














NoteHow the code works





qtm(shp, fill)                                            # tmap

qtm() (quick thematic map) draws a choropleth map in one call, with default classes, colours and legend. The second argument names the column that sets the colour of each township.




It then maps the number of households beside the number of households with a radio.

TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_fill(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Total households")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_fill(fill = "RADIO",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Number Radio")) +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map,
             asp = NA, ncol = 2)














NoteHow the code works





The block uses six functions:
tm_shape(shp)                                             # tmap
tm_fill(fill, fill.scale, fill.legend)                    # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(n, style)                              # tmap
tm_legend(title)                                          # tmap
tm_borders(col_alpha)                                     # tmap
tmap_arrange(..., asp, ncol)                              # tmap

tm_shape() names the sf object that the layers after it draw, and each + adds a layer.
tm_fill() colours each township by the column named in fill, without drawing its outline. tm_borders() draws the outlines as a separate layer, at half opacity.
tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks") divides the values into five classes by the Jenks natural breaks method, which places the class boundaries where the gaps between the sorted values are largest.
tmap_arrange() places the two stored maps side by side. asp = NA lets each map keep the shape of Shan State.

The chapter is written for tmap version 3, and the installed version is 4, which renames some arguments. The chapter’s code and the version used here:







Chapter (tmap 3)
This page (tmap 4)




tm_fill(col = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS", n = 5, style = "jenks", title = "Total households")
tm_fill(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS", fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 5, style = "jenks"), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Total households"))


tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)
tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)



tmap 4 still accepts the chapter’s version 3 code, but it translates tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) into a half-transparent fill, which pales the whole map. col_alpha applies the transparency to the borders, which is what the chapter intends.



The chapter then draws the number of households beside the radio penetration rate, as one map with two panels.

tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks"),
              fill.free = TRUE) +
  tm_facets(ncol = 2)














NoteHow the code works






Given two column names in fill, tm_polygons() draws one panel for each, and tm_facets(ncol = 2) places the panels side by side. fill.free = TRUE gives each panel its own classes and legend, because the two columns are on different scales.
The chapter’s version 3 code is tm_polygons(c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"), style = "jenks") + tm_facets(sync = TRUE, ncol = 2).




The first pair of maps shows that the count of radios follows the number of households: the townships in the darkest class are largely the same on both maps. The chapter’s question is what differs between the two panels. The highest radio rates are along the western edge of the state, from the north-west to the south-west, with one more township in the east. Several of the townships with the most households, such as the darkest township in the north of the left-hand panel, have only moderate rates. Dividing by the number of households removes the effect of township size.
Three features of the maps are used later on this page:







Feature of the maps
Used in




The map of radio counts has much the same pattern as the map of households
2.3, the reason for using rates


The highest radio rates are along the western edge of the state
4.1: radio is one of the two rates with significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I 0.44). 4.8: the “High radio” region of REDCAP is on the western edge, and seven of the ten highest radio rates are in it


Households are concentrated in a few large townships, Taunggyi the largest with 82,604
4.5 and 4.7: a minimum number of households per region. Taunggyi meets the minimum of 50,000 in section 4.5 on its own





3.1.3 Correlation between the variables
Two variables that are highly correlated measure much the same thing. If both enter the clustering, that dimension is counted twice. In section 12.6, the correlations are checked before the variables are chosen.

cluster_vars.cor <- cor(ict_derived[, 12:17])
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,
               lower = "ellipse",
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")














NoteHow the code works





The block uses two functions:
cor(x)                                                    # stats
corrplot.mixed(corr, lower, upper, tl.pos, diag, tl.col)  # corrplot

cor() returns the matrix of Pearson correlations between every pair of columns.
ict_derived[, 12:17] picks part of the table. Square brackets after a table take the form table[rows, columns]. Nothing before the comma means every row, all 55 townships. 12:17 after the comma is the sequence 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, which means columns 12 to 17: the six penetration rates, as the column table in section 2.3 shows. cor() accepts numbers only, so the name and code columns (1 to 4) and the counts (5 to 11) are left out.
corrplot.mixed() draws the matrix in two halves. lower = "ellipse" draws each correlation below the diagonal as an ellipse, narrower for a stronger correlation, and tilted right for a positive one. upper = "number" prints the coefficient above the diagonal. tl.pos = "lt" puts the variable names on the left and top, diag = "l" draws the diagonal in the style of the lower half, and tl.col sets the colour of the names.




Computer and internet are correlated at 0.87, the highest pair. The chapter keeps computer and drops internet. TV, mobile phone and computer are also correlated with each other at about 0.7. Radio is nearly uncorrelated with the others, and is negatively correlated with land line (−0.31).






NoteWhy one of two highly correlated variables is dropped



Euclidean distance adds one squared difference for each variable. Computer and internet ownership are high in the same townships, so a difference on one is usually a difference on the other, and the same difference is counted twice.
Each method in Part 1 was run twice on the raw rates, once without internet, as in the chapter, and once with it. An adjusted Rand index of 1 would mean the same six clusters both times (the index is explained in section 4.2).








Section
Use of the Euclidean distance
Adjusted Rand index, without and with internet




3.1 Hierarchical clustering
the two closest clusters are merged at each step
0.78


3.2 SKATER
the minimum spanning tree is built from the edge costs, and each cut reduces the within-region sum of squares
0.95


3.3 ClustGeo, α = 0.2
D0, the variable part of the criterion
0.42



The distances themselves change very little: the two distance matrices are correlated at 0.9998. The clusters change more, because they are weakly separated (section 4.4). A small change in the distances can change which two clusters are merged first, and every later merge depends on that one. SKATER changes least, because nearly the same edges are in its minimum spanning tree both times.
In the chapter, internet is dropped at a correlation of 0.87, and the pairs at about 0.7, such as TV and mobile phone (0.72), are kept. No threshold is given in the chapter.




3.1.4 The clustering variables
The clustering functions take a plain table of numbers: one row per township and one column per variable, with no geometry and no text columns. This step builds that table from shan_sf, keeps the five rates chosen in section 3.1.3, and uses the township names as row names, so that the dendrogram in section 3.1.10 labels each leaf with its township.

cluster_vars <- shan_sf |>
  st_set_geometry(NULL) |>
  select("TS.x", "RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR", "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR")
row.names(cluster_vars) <- cluster_vars$"TS.x"
shan_ict <- select(cluster_vars, c(2:6))

st_set_geometry(x, NULL)                                  # sf

select() keeps the township name and five of the rates, leaving out INTERNET_PR.

NoteWhy the township is the unit of analysis



Each row of shan_ict is one township. The township name can label the rows because no two townships share a name. A district name is shared by several townships, so it cannot label the rows.
The township is also the most detailed level in the data. The maps show computer ownership at three levels on one colour scale. A district or part of the state has the rate of all its households together.









When townships are combined into districts, the differences between them are lost: Taunggyi township, at 81 computers per thousand households, is in a district with a rate of 33.




3.1.5 Standardisation
The clustering methods below measure how far apart two townships are with Euclidean distance, the square root of the sum of squared differences across the variables. A variable with a larger spread contributes larger squared differences. Sections 12.7.3 and 12.7.4 compute two standardised versions of the variables.

summary(shan_ict.std)
